#46564. More on Dota 2

📅 16 Aug 2017 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (83 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

More on Dota 2

📅 16 Aug 2017 | ⏱️ 1 min read (83 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Our Dota 2 result highlights that self-play can catapult the performance of machine learning systems from far below human level to superhuman, given sufficient compute. In the span of a month, our system went from barely matching a high-ranked player to beating the top pros and has continued to improve since then. Supervised deep learning systems can only be as good as their training datasets, but in self-play systems, the available data improves automatically as the agent gets better.

📖 Baca

OpenAI Baselines: ACKTR & A2C

📅 18 Aug 2017 | ⏱️ 1 min read (54 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’re releasing two new OpenAI Baselines implementations: ACKTR and A2C. A2C is a synchronous, deterministic variant of Asynchronous Advantage Actor Critic (A3C) which we’ve found gives equal performance. ACKTR is a more sample-efficient reinforcement learning algorithm than TRPO and A2C, and requires only slightly more computation than A2C per revision.

#46437. Industry News: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm

📅 07 Mar 2018 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (91 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm

📅 07 Mar 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (91 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that we’ve developed a simple meta-learning algorithm called Reptile which works by repeatedly sampling a task, performing stochastic gradient descent on it, and updating the initial parameters towards the final parameters learned on that task. Reptile is the application of the Shortest Descent algorithm to the meta-learning setting, and is mathematically similar to first-order MAML (which is a version of the well-known MAML algorithm) that only needs black-box access to an optimizer such as SGD or Adam, with similar computational efficiency and performance.

📅 18 Apr 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (75 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, we’re releasing an experimental metalearning approach called Evolved Policy Gradients, a method that evolves the loss function of learning agents, which can enable fast training on novel tasks. Agents trained with EPG can succeed at basic tasks at test time that were outside their training regime, like learning to navigate to an object on a different side of the room from where it was placed during training.

Industry News: AI and compute

📅 16 May 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (91 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012, the amount of compute used in the largest AI training runs has been increasing exponentially with a 3.4-month doubling time (by comparison, Moore’s Law had a 2-year doubling period)[^footnote-correction]. Since 2012, this metric has grown by more than 300,000x (a 2-year doubling period would yield only a 7x increase). Improvements in compute have been a key component of AI progress, so as long as this trend continues, it’s worth preparing for the implications of systems far outside today’s capabilities.

Industry News: Learning Montezuma’s Revenge from a single demonstration

📅 04 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (68 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’ve trained an agent to achieve a high score of 74,500 on Montezuma’s Revenge from a single human demonstration, better than any previously published result. Our algorithm is simple: the agent plays a sequence of games starting from carefully chosen states from the demonstration, and learns from them by optimizing the game score using PPO, the same reinforcement learning algorithm that underpins OpenAI Five.

Glow: Better reversible generative models

📅 09 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (71 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We introduce Glow, a reversible generative model which uses invertible 1x1 convolutions. It extends previous work on reversible generative models and simplifies the architecture. Our model can generate realistic high resolution images, supports efficient sampling, and discovers features that can be used to manipulate attributes of data. We’re releasing code for the model and an online visualization tool so people can explore and build on these results.
